title: Sung in the gurdwara
hook: the Rehat Maryada allows only Gurbani and the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal for kirtan
tomorrow: Reading a pauri of Bhai Gurdas

segments.voice: Yesterday, langar: Nand Lal's kitchen fed a stranger at the wrong hour, and the stranger was the Guru. Your line was serve anytime.

A line sung on Sunday turns up again on Tuesday, at the sink, or halfway through the drive to work. Sung words don't stay in the room where they were sung. That makes a plain question matter in a gurdwara: which words get to be sung there? Plenty of poems have been written about the Gurus. The Sikh code of conduct gives a short, clear answer, and two names from this block are in it. Today: Rehat Maryada.
screen: `A LINE SUNG ON SUNDAY, HUMMED ON TUESDAY.` → `SUNG WORDS TRAVEL.` → `WHICH WORDS GET TO BE SUNG?`

segments.voice: The code is the Sikh Rehat Maryada, published by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee. In its section on kirtan, it says that in the congregation, only Gurbani, the Guru's own hymns, may be sung, along with the compositions that explain it: the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal. That's the whole list. Other poems about the Gurus, many of them beautiful, aren't called bad. They're simply kept out of kirtan in the sangat. Look at how the code treats the two poets: not as extra scripture standing beside the Guru, but as a key to it. Their words are allowed because they help open the Gurbani. Bhai Gurdas, the scribe, with his vars full of pictures: the sun rising and the stars going out, the cup of milk at Multan. Bhai Nand Lal, the poet at Guru Gobind Singh's court, with his Persian ghazals of longing. One wrote in Punjabi and Braj, the other in Persian. Very different voices, both in. So in a gurdwara, when the ragis start a piece, they sing Gurbani: in the code's own terms, hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib and the hymns of Guru Gobind Singh. Sometimes the ragi announces that a var of Bhai Gurdas or a ghazal of Bhai Nand Lal is coming. That's the code at work: the Guru's word at the center, and two trusted servants allowed to stand nearby and explain it. Some readers hear a wider lesson in this: what gets repeated becomes part of the one who repeats it.
screen: `THE SIKH REHAT MARYADA ON KIRTAN.` · `GURBANI, AND TWO WHO EXPLAIN IT.` · `A SCRIBE AND A PERSIAN POET.` · `LISTEN FOR THEIR NAMES.` · then, large: `THE TWO VOICES ALLOWED.`

segments.voice: Next time you hear kirtan, in a gurdwara or on a stream, listen for whether the ragi names Bhai Gurdas or Bhai Nand Lal before a piece begins. For now, let the sounds around you come in, the fridge, the street, a voice in another room, and notice which ones you'd let in on purpose and which just arrive. Then ask which words you repeat most often in a day.
Rehat Maryada, the Sikh code of conduct that allows Gurbani and the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal in kirtan because they explain it.
Your line: the two voices allowed. The Guru's word at the center, and two servants close by. Day seven hundred eighteen, done.
